Built-Up Roofing (BUR): A Complete Owner's Reference

What built-up (tar-and-gravel) roofing is, why it still protects long-hold buildings, service life and cost realities, failure modes, and owner verification points.

Editorially reviewed Editorial review: Hila Atlan, Founder & Editor-in-Chief Updated July 21, 2026 5 sources cited 2 min read Editorial standards · Report an error

Key takeaways

  • BUR is the century-old multi-ply system: alternating bitumen and reinforcing felts, usually gravel-surfaced — maximum redundancy.
  • Trade guidance consistently plans well-built BUR at 20–30 years, with 4-ply systems toward the high end; the aging is gradual, not sudden.
  • Its weaknesses are weight, installation odor/logistics, and a shrinking specialist labor base.
  • For owners, BUR decisions today are usually about maintaining or replacing existing BUR, not specifying new.

What BUR is

Built-up roofing is the original low-slope system: three to five alternating layers of bitumen and reinforcing felt, finished with aggregate (gravel), a mineral cap sheet, or a reflective coating. The redundancy is structural to the concept — water must find a path through every ply.

Where it fits

New BUR specification has narrowed to owners and institutions that prize its proven longevity and abuse-tolerance (campuses, government, industrial) and regions that retain strong BUR crews. For everyone else, the practical BUR questions are about the roof you already have: how to maintain it, when to coat it, and what replaces it.

How it performs

AttributeTypical performanceWhat drives variance
Service life20–30 years (4-ply toward the high end)Ply count, drainage, maintenance
RedundancyHighest of common systemsPly count
WeightHigh (especially graveled)Structure must carry it
RepairabilityHigh — mature techniquesAging labor base
EnergyPoor unless coated/white-cappedSurfacing

Decision framework (for existing BUR)

  1. Condition first. Core cuts and a moisture survey tell you whether the plies are dry. Dry BUR is a maintenance asset; saturated BUR is a replacement conversation.
  2. Coat or not. Sound but UV-tired BUR is a strong coating candidate.
  3. Replacement path. When BUR retires, structure (weight capacity), insulation upgrades, and code-required attachment usually push replacement toward mod-bit or single-ply — get the structural analysis before the bids.

Common failure modes

  • Membrane fatigue and alligatoring of exposed bitumen.
  • Blistering from interply moisture.
  • Gravel displacement exposing felts (and hiding damage from inspectors).
  • Flashing failure — as everywhere, the details lead.
  • Ponding-accelerated decay — see ponding water.

Cost considerations

New BUR is labor-intensive and often the most expensive common system first-cost; its defense is cost-per-service-year on long holds. Maintenance and coating economics are typically favorable because the substrate tolerates work so well. Regional installed-cost ranges vary too widely to state a single national figure honestly; request full-assembly quotes with identical ply counts and surfacing before comparing.

Maintenance guidance

Annual professional inspection plus post-storm checks; keep gravel evenly distributed; watch drains for granule/gravel migration; address exposed felts immediately; maintain flashings aggressively — BUR fields outlive their details.

Frequently asked questions

Our BUR is 25 years old and doesn’t leak. Replace it? Not on age alone. Commission a moisture survey and core sample. Dry, adhered BUR at 25 can have real life left — and is often coatable. Run Repair or Replace with data, not anniversaries.

Is gravel on the roof a problem? No — surfacing aggregate is part of the system (UV and fire protection). Displaced or missing gravel is the problem to flag.

Why are BUR bids so different from each other? Ply count, surfacing, tear-off scope, and insulation are frequently unequal across bids. Force identical specifications before comparing numbers.

Sources

  1. ASTM D312/D312M — Standard Specification for Asphalt Used in Roofing — ASTM InternationalConfirms the roofing asphalt (bitumen) in built-up roofs is a standardized material classified in four types (I–IV). Verified against the current ASTM catalogue entry (D312/D312M-16a, reapproved 2023). A material specification for the asphalt only — it does not establish BUR service life or assembly performance.
  2. ASTM D2178/D2178M — Standard Specification for Asphalt Glass Felt Used in Roofing and Waterproofing — ASTM InternationalThe reinforcing-ply half of a built-up roof: asphalt-impregnated glass felt, specified for use with D312 asphalt in BUR construction. Verified against the current ASTM catalogue entry (D2178/D2178M-15a, reapproved 2021). Specifies the felt material, not the finished roof's longevity.
  3. Advantages of Multi-Ply Built-Up Roofing (Fast Facts) — Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association (industry association)Multi-layer construction and the redundancy argument — 'if the top layer is damaged, the subsequent layers underneath provide a back-up layer to stop water' — plus the cost-per-year-of-service framing and the note that cold-applied systems reduce fume exposure. Manufacturer-association literature: promotional in purpose and contains no service-life figures.
  4. BUR Multi-Ply Built-Up Roofing — Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association (industry association)Surfacing options (reflective coating, white granulated cap sheet, asphalt flood coat, fibered aluminum coating) and BUR's UL Class A fire rating. Manufacturer-association literature; states no service-life numbers.
  5. Built-Up Roof Life Expectancy: How Long Will Your BUR Last — East Penn Roofing (trade/vendor summary)Cited only as an example of commonly published trade guidance for the 20–30 year planning range and the ply-count correlation (3-ply toward 15–20 years, 4-ply 20–30, 5-ply beyond). Vendor-published commentary, not independent research. As with other membrane families, no independent longitudinal field study of BUR service life is public — the range is trade consensus, not measured data.
